name: PT Avia Avian Tbk

frontmatter.title: Avia Avian: the paint leader priced for a decline
frontmatter.summary: Avia Avian is Indonesia's largest decorative paint maker and it trades as though the business were shrinking. Nine months of 2026 showed price-led revenue growth with flat volume, a margin held through an oil shock, and more cash than debt. We initiate at BUY with a target of Rp413, 43.8% above the last paid price.
thesis: The franchise is intact and the price does not reflect it: management's own estimate of 26.0% of the national market, 150 centres in its own network and a gross margin that held through the Iran-conflict oil spike [S3, S5, S6].
The market is discounting a permanent contraction: the reverse DCF says today's Rp304 requires revenue growth of -2.1% in every forecast year to FY2035E, against our 7.0% [S0, S6].
The balance sheet is the floor: debt of 86.2 IDR bn against cash that more than covers it, the shares at 9.4 times forward earnings, and capex at only 6.2% of revenue [S2, S3].

Cash returns are real and committed: an interim dividend of Rp12.0/share already declared for 2026, a stated policy floor of 50.0% of distributable profit, and a buyback authorised for up to 1,425 m shares [S6, S7].
The risk is that the 2026 price increases unwind faster than input costs do, which is the bear case at Rp324 rather than our base case at Rp413 [S3, S6].

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Avia Avian Tbk with a BUY rating and a twelve-month target of Rp413, which is 43.8% above the Rp304 at which the shares last traded [S0]. The company makes and distributes decorative paint and complementary building products in Indonesia, sells through company-owned distribution centres into a fragmented trade, and carries a net cash balance rather than debt [S3, S6]. On our numbers it earns a return on equity of 18.2% through a cycle in which input costs moved violently, and it converts most of that profit into cash [S2, S3].

The disagreement with the price is not narrow and it is not a matter of degree. At Rp304 the shares are valued at 9.4 times our FY2026E earnings and 5.3 times EBITDA, and a reverse DCF on our own assumptions says the price is only justified if revenue falls at -2.1% a year in every forecast year to FY2035E - a permanent contraction - rather than the 7.0% growth we forecast [S0]. We think that is the wrong reading of 2026. The nine months showed revenue ahead of the prior year on price with architectural volume up only 3.5%, and that came after a discounting year in which revenue grew more slowly than production [S3, S5, F1, F2]. We deliberately do not extrapolate the price year, and we forecast 7.0% for FY2027E as volume returns to the industry rate [S6].

Three things move the value from here. The first is whether the gross margin holds as the deck's Brent path falls from US$96.0/bbl toward US$75.0/bbl. The nine months of 2026 show the cost was recovered in price; the open question is whether that recovery survives when the cost itself falls and the trade channel has less reason to accept the higher shelf price [S3] [d.oil.brent]. The second is the Cirebon plant and whether the capacity arrives into demand rather than into a price war against imports [S6, S8]. The third is capital return: at a 7.9% forward dividend yield and a buyback already authorised, the shares pay an owner to wait [S0, S6].

Decorative paint is a deceptively simple business that rewards scale in three places: pigment and resin purchasing, the density of the retail network, and the cost of getting a heavy, low-value liquid to thousands of small shops. Brand matters because the buyer is usually a householder or a contractor repainting an existing wall, and the colour card at the shop counter is the point of sale. It is also a business where the incumbent's advantage compounds slowly and erodes slowly, which is why paint leaders in most emerging markets hold share for decades while competing mostly on service and shelf presence rather than on price.

PT Avia Avian Tbk, which trades as Avian Brands, manufactures architectural coatings and a wide portfolio of related building products and sells them in Indonesia under brands that include Avitex, No Drop and Avian [S6, S0]. The product range runs from interior and exterior wall paint through waterproofing, wood and iron coatings, primers and putty to tile adhesive, grout, sealant and the brushes and rollers that go with them, so the company sells a basket to the same shop counter rather than a single product line [S0]. Manufacturing sits at Sidoarjo in East Java and Serang in Banten, with a third site at Cirebon coming into service [S6].

The company reports two segments. Architectural solutions took 5,367 IDR bn of the 6,918 IDR bn of revenue booked in the nine months to 30 September 2026, and trading goods took 1,550 IDR bn, which makes this overwhelmingly a coatings business with a smaller distribution arm attached to it [S3]. Gross profit is not split by segment in the interim filing, but the trading line is a resale business with materially lower margins and it is the smaller of the two, so the economics of the group follow the paint [S3].

Capacity is the constraint the company itself flags. Sidoarjo can produce 214 kt a year and Serang 72.6 kt, and utilisation of the two reached 76.0% against a stated ideal ceiling of eighty per cent, which is why the third plant exists [S6]. Production was 227 kt in 2025 against 197 kt in the prior year, so the existing lines are close to full and the increment has to come from Cirebon, whose eventual capacity is 225 kt [S6]. The ramp of that plant is therefore the single most important operational variable in the forecast, and we treat it as a schedule risk rather than as a demand risk [S6].

Distribution is the asset that is hardest to replicate. The company added three company-owned distribution centres in the third quarter of 2026 to reach 150 centres, and management describes the expansion as improving availability and delivery speed rather than as a cost programme [S5]. Those centres sit in front of a long tail of independent paint shops, project buyers and modern retail, and they are the reason a new entrant cannot simply buy shelf space with a cheaper can of paint [S5, S6]. Management puts its national market share at 26.0% on its own internal estimate, against industry consumption of 1.3 Mt a year [S6]. The two numbers do not measure the same thing and we do not treat them as if they did: production of 227 kt against consumption of 1.3 Mt is a materially smaller share of the market on a volume basis, so the 26.0% has to be read as management's own estimate of its position - most plausibly a value share, or a share of the branded segment - rather than as a volume share of the whole market [S6, F1, F8].

The growth strategy has three visible legs. The first is product cadence: the company launched a steady stream of new products through 2026, including two in the third quarter alone, which defends shelf space and supports price [S5]. The second is adjacency: in early 2025 it took a minority stake in an adhesives producer whose brands sit naturally beside paint in the same shop, buying into a category rather than building it [S6]. The third is capital return, where an extraordinary shareholders' meeting in April 2025 authorised a buyback of up to 1,425 m shares and the company has been buying [S6].

Ownership is concentrated and family-based. Two family holding companies, PT Wahana Lancar Rejeki and PT Tancorp Surya Sentosa, are disclosed as the controlling shareholders, and three family members are named as the ultimate beneficial owners [S6]. Insiders hold 81.4% of the register and the free float is 13.3%, a structure that explains both the low liquidity in normal times and the sensitivity of the shares to index and free-float rules [S0, S6].

Paint manufacturing is a mixing business rather than a chemical one. The plant buys titanium dioxide for whiteness and opacity, calcium carbonate as filler, resins and emulsions as the binder, and solvents and additives to control flow and drying, then blends them to a formulation and fills cans. The capital intensity is modest relative to the value of the brand, which is why a leader can fund expansion from operating cash flow and still pay out most of its profit. The binding constraints are usually the colour-matching service at the dealer and the working capital tied up in inventory across a long tail of stock-keeping units.

Indonesia consumes 1.3 Mt of paint a year, which the industry association puts at a little over four kilogrammes per head, well below the intensity of Thailand and Malaysia and therefore with room to grow as incomes and housing stock rise [S8, S6]. The annual report projects industry growth of 6.5% a year across the period to 2032, a rate that sits above the deck's long-run inflation rate and therefore implies real volume growth, and well below what a low per-capita starting point would allow if property completions recovered [S6] [d.macro.cpi_id]. We treat that projection as the ceiling for a volume-led year rather than as the base case for the market as a whole, because the association's own account of recent years is one of stagnation [S8].

Demand is driven by three things that move on different clocks. New housing and property completions set the new-build volume; the repaint cycle, which is the larger part of the market in a country with an established housing stock, sets the recurring volume and is far less cyclical; and government infrastructure, including the new capital project, sets the project channel, which the association says has slowed [S8]. The macro deck has real GDP growth at 5.3 rate and inflation at 3.3 rate, a combination that supports nominal paint demand in the middle single digits without producing a boom [d.macro.gdp_real_id] [d.macro.cpi_id].

The cost side is where the industry's fortunes actually swing. Raw materials are the largest line in cost of goods sold, and the oil-linked part of the basket moves with Brent, which the deck has at US$96.0/bbl for FY2026E after a conflict-driven spike, falling to US$84.0/bbl and then a long run of US$75.0/bbl [d.oil.brent]. The nine months of 2026 are the natural experiment: raw-material costs rose sharply under the Iran conflict, and Avia Avian still reported a gross margin level with the prior full year, which tells us the industry as a whole succeeded in repricing rather than absorbing the cost [S3, S5].

Competition is fragmented at the bottom and concentrated at the top. Management estimates a national share of 26.0%, which makes Avia Avian the leader by a wide margin in decorative paint, with the rest split among a long tail of regional producers and, increasingly, imported finished paint [S6, S8]. The producers' association has asked the government to restrict imports of finished paint on the argument that local capacity can make every category, and it points to the rupiah as the channel through which imports became cheaper [S8]. The rupiah is at Rp18,080/USD against the dollar in the deck, weaker than the prior-year average, so the pressure is live [d.macro.usd_idr].

On the five-forces reading, the industry is more attractive than its fragmentation suggests. Supplier power is moderate and concentrated in titanium dioxide and resin, but the leader makes part of its own resin and buys at a scale the tail cannot match [S6]. Buyer power at the shop counter is low because the brand, not the shop, carries the decision, though project buyers and modern retail negotiate harder. The threat of new entrants is low at national scale and high at the regional level, where a single plant and a distributor can serve one province. Substitutes are limited to alternative finishes in specific applications. Rivalry is the real force, and it is expressed as discounting in the trade channel rather than as capacity wars, because the incumbents already own the plants [S6, S8].

The moat is therefore a combination rather than a single advantage: a brand that households recognise, a distribution network of 150 centres that a challenger would have to replicate, manufacturing scale at 227 kt of output, and partial self-supply of resin [S5, S6]. None of those is unassailable on its own. Together they explain why the leader has held a share in the mid-twenties through a decade of import competition and why its gross margin has stayed in the mid-forties rather than converging on the industry average [S3, S6].

Policy is the swing external factor. The association's request for import restrictions, if granted, would remove the price ceiling that imported paint imposes on the trade channel; if refused, the discounting continues [S8]. The other policy lever is the exchange rate, since a weaker rupiah raises the cost of imported pigment and resin as well as the competitiveness of imports, and the deck has the rupiah drifting weaker through the forecast [S8] [d.macro.usd_idr].

Paint demand in emerging markets tracks household formation more closely than it tracks GDP, because a new house needs far more paint than an existing one and a repaint is deferred rather than cancelled when incomes tighten. That asymmetry makes volumes sticky in a downturn and slow to recover afterwards, and it is why paint makers tend to trade at a premium to construction materials through a cycle even when their end market is the same building. The premium disappears when a market is flooded with imports that compete on price alone.

All figures in IDR bn unless stated. The historical record is one of steady compounding interrupted by the pandemic and then by a cost shock. Revenue ran from 6,694.2 in FY2022A to 8,123.7 in FY2025A, EBITDA from 1,657.4 to 2,156.6, and net profit to the parent from 1,400.6 to 1,747.5, with the net margin at 21.5% in FY2025A and a return on equity of 18.2% [S0, S2]. Throughout that period the company carried no bank debt and a cash balance that exceeded its lease liabilities many times over, so the earnings were not levered [S2].

The nine months to September 2026 are the most informative period in the file. Revenue reached 6,918 IDR bn against the prior year's comparable, profit for the period was 1,384 IDR bn, and operating cash flow was 1,689 IDR bn, which is more cash than profit [S3]. Gross margin held at the prior year's level even though raw materials rose under the Iran conflict, and the tax charge of 389 IDR bn on pre-tax profit implies an effective rate close to the statutory one rather than the lower rate FY2025 enjoyed from prior-year adjustments [S3, S2]. The fourth quarter is the only part of FY2026E we have to build, and we do it from the third quarter's run-rate grossed up for the seasonal step-up the prior year showed between those two quarters, which gives FY2026E revenue of 9,415.4 and growth of 15.9% [S3, S2].

That growth is almost entirely price. Architectural volume rose 3.5% in the nine months, so the gap between volume and revenue is repricing; that attribution is our inference from the revenue and volume numbers, not a company statement, because the sources report the volume growth without attributing it [S5, F21]. We have deliberately refused to carry that into FY2027E: a price year is a one-off reset, not a growth rate, and forecasting 7.0% assumes volume returns to roughly the industry rate plus a modest share gain from Cirebon capacity [S5, S6]. Growth then tapers to 7.0%, 6.5% and 6.0%, and to 4.5% in the long run [S6].

Margins are modelled through two cost links rather than through a house view on pricing, and the links are deliberately small. Raw materials were 1,967 IDR bn of the 3,858 IDR bn of cost of goods sold in the nine months, just over half, and only the resin, emulsion and solvent content of that basket tracks oil, so we expose 25.0% of cost of goods sold to Brent at a 92.0% pass-through, and a further 15.0% to the rupiah at 90.0% for the imported pigment and resin content [S3, S8]. The pass-through is not fitted to a single year. Across the four annual Brent moves in FY2022-FY2026 the margin change regresses on the Brent change with a slope of a little over one percentage point of margin per hundred per cent of Brent and almost no explanatory power: oil explains essentially none of the margin history, and the FY2023 gain on the Brent fall cannot be produced by any share of cost of goods sold at a pass-through below complete [S0, S2, d.oil.brent]. We therefore do not claim the link reproduces FY2023; we attribute that year to post-IPO mix and pricing, and we set the pair to the identified sensitivity rather than to the outlier. The practical reading is complete pass-through with a small residual, which is what the nine months of 2026 show: the margin held at 44.2% through a large Brent rise because the cost was recovered in price [S3, S2]. On that basis the gross margin is 44.2% in FY2026E and drifts to 44.5% by FY2030E as the deck's Brent falls, and with selling and administrative costs held at 20.4% of revenue the EBIT margin is 23.8% and EBITDA 2,526.2 [S2, S3].

The fourth quarter of 2026 is the one quarter we have to build, and we build it at the nine-month run-rate margin rather than at the FY2025 fourth-quarter step-up. The revenue seasonal is a demand pattern - trade stocking ahead of the year-end - and we apply it; the margin step-up is a single observation, and the nine-month figure already contains the 2026 price and mix, so carrying the step-up as well would double-count the repricing [S3, S2]. If the FY2025 fourth-quarter margin repeated, FY2026E gross profit would be higher and the year's margin above the nine-month actual; that is an upside we do not model and the bull case carries.

FY2025 is the year the report has to be honest about, because it is the best argument against the 2026 price level. Production rose from 197 kt to 227 kt while revenue rose from 7,471.4 to 8,123.7: revenue grew more slowly than volume, so realised price and mix fell in a year when Brent itself fell [S2, F1, F2, d.oil.brent]. That is the opposite of 2026, when revenue rose faster than volume, and it means 2026 is a rebound off a discounting year rather than evidence of a new pricing plateau. It is also a direct test of the pass-through: if price fell faster than cost in FY2025, pass-through was incomplete in that year, which is why the bear case carries a partial give-back of the 2026 increases.

Cash conversion is the strongest part of the story and the part most easily overstated. Capital expenditure ran at 6.2% of revenue in FY2025A, and 477 IDR bn of expenditure was contracted at the end of 2025 against a much smaller figure a year earlier, so the build is real and funded from cash [S6, S2]. That contracted Cirebon commitment is why we carry capex above the nine-month run-rate for the full year rather than tapering it to the cash actually spent by September: the commitment is on the balance sheet, the spend is scheduled, and the plant is the capacity the growth case needs. Depreciation and amortisation is modelled at 3.0% of revenue, above the data pack's ratio because the notes show a larger charge once right-of-use depreciation of 98.7 IDR bn and fixed-asset depreciation of 165 IDR bn are added together [S2, S0]. Working capital is held at 27.0% of revenue, close to the historical ratio, and the resulting free cash flow to the firm is 1,120.1 in FY2026E and 1,907.0 by FY2030E [S0].

The balance sheet is the reason the equity is worth more than the operating business alone. Cash and short-term investments were 4,224.9 IDR bn against debt of 86.2 IDR bn, so net debt was -4,138.7 and net debt to EBITDA was -1.9 [S2, S0]. Finance income was 159 IDR bn in the nine months, a meaningful slice of pre-tax profit, and we model a yield of 4.7% on opening cash because the bond portfolio was rolled into deposits during the year [S3, S2]. Capital allocation is conservative to a fault: the dividend policy floor is 50.0% of distributable profit, the FY2026E payout in our model is 75.0%, the interim dividend already declared is Rp12.0/share, and the buyback authorisation covers 1,425 m shares [S6, S7]. One convention needs stating: the data pack's FY2025A dividend per share of 12.0 and the 40.7% payout it implies pick up only the April-2026 final instalment, whereas the year's declared dividends were the November-2025 interim plus that final, which is the payout the annual report shows and is well above the 50.0% policy floor; the forecast is unaffected, but the historical line understates the payout and the yield [S0, S6].

Earnings quality deserves three flags. The good flag is accruals: operating cash flow of 1,689 IDR bn ran ahead of profit of 1,384 IDR bn in the nine months, so the earnings are cash-backed and the accrual component is negative [S3]. The caution flag is inventory, which stood at 2,234 IDR bn at the end of September against a much lower balance at the prior year-end, a build that is consistent with restocking ahead of price increases but also with slower sell-through at the dealer level [S3]. The third flag is related-party purchasing: 42.2% of cost of goods sold was bought from related parties in the nine months, which is a structural feature of a family-controlled group rather than a surprise, but it is the item we would test hardest if margins ever diverged from the industry's [S3, S6]. The data pack's depreciation line is also lower than the notes imply, which we disclose rather than paper over [S0, S2].

We value the company on free cash flow to the firm as the primary method, with EV/EBITDA and P/E cross-checks, weighted 60.0%, 25.0% and 15.0% [S0]. The method set fits a business that is capital-light relative to its brand, has no leverage, and returns most of its cash: the discounted cash flow captures the terminal value of a franchise, while the multiples anchor the answer to what comparable chemical and coatings assets change hands for. A dividend discount model would also fit a business with a high payout and a surplus balance sheet, and we do not weight one: the dividend is capped by the payout policy and by the net cash sitting outside the operating business, so a Gordon model on the dividend alone would value the cash return and not the franchise. It is a useful sanity check on the cash flow answer rather than a competing method, and at our own cost of equity and terminal growth it lands near the price rather than at the DCF, which is the tension section five carries.

The cost of capital is built from the deck and the engine's country convention, and the full build is printed here so it can be checked. The rupiah risk-free rate is 7.4%. The engine deducts the 1.6% Indonesian default spread from it, because the country risk premium below already prices that risk and adding both would double-count it. It then adds a levered beta of 0.90 - the unlevered 0.90 levered at a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.13% - multiplied by the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the country risk premium of 2.5%. That is a cost of equity of 11.9% [S0]. The pre-tax cost of debt the engine uses is 9.4%, the risk-free rate plus a corporate spread rather than the lease rate in the filing; at a 0.13% debt weight it makes the weighted average cost of capital 11.9% [S2, S3]. Adding the default spread back would raise the cost of equity by the spread itself, and the higher-WACC column of the sensitivity table is the nearest stress to that: it still values the shares well above the price, so the rating does not depend on the country convention. The terminal growth rate is 4.0%, below the rupiah cap and below every explicit-year growth rate, so the model decelerates into perpetuity rather than accelerating.

The discounted cash flow produces a value of Rp456 per share on an enterprise value of 22,328 IDR bn, to which the net cash position is added to reach equity value [S0]. That net cash is the 30 September 2026 position from the latest filing - cash and cash equivalents of 3,678 IDR bn plus short-term investments of 954 IDR bn less lease liabilities - and not the 30 June data-pack figure, which it supersedes: the September balance sheet is the stronger of the two, because the nine months generated operating cash flow well ahead of profit, so the bridge and the forecast are now on the same date and the difference works in the shares' favour rather than against them [S3, S0]. Half the value, 51.4%, sits in the terminal value, which is normal for a business growing in the middle single digits with a high cash conversion and is the part of the answer we stress hardest. Free cash flow to the firm rises from 1,120.1 in FY2026E to 2,413.8 in the final explicit year, driven by revenue growth rather than by margin expansion, which is the conservative choice in a business that has just shown it can hold a margin.

The two cross-checks are far below the primary method, and we do not dismiss that. EV/EBITDA gives Rp312 at a peer median of 5.4 times, -31.6% from the discounted cash flow, and the P/E cross-check gives Rp264 at 8.0 times, -42.1% away [S0]. Three things explain the gap and only one of them is a warning. First, both multiples are struck on the last actual year rather than on a forward year, and that is deliberate: the peer medians are themselves trailing multiples computed from the peers' trailing metrics, so applying them to our forward earnings would mix a trailing multiple with a forward metric and double-count the growth the cash flow already carries [S0]. On FY2026E metrics the same peer medians would give values above the discounted cash flow, so the trailing basis is the conservative one and it is what keeps the cross-checks in the blend as a floor rather than as a competing value. Second, the peer set is a mixed bag of Indonesian basic-materials names with lower margins and heavier capital needs than a coatings leader, so the median multiple is a low anchor for this business. Third, and genuinely a warning, a coatings franchise that grows in the middle single digits with a high payout rarely trades at single-digit EV/EBITDA in a functioning market, so if the peer multiple is the right lens then the shares are fairly valued at best.

We take the gap seriously by leaning on the cash flow but refusing to ignore the multiples. The weighted target of Rp413 is what the blend produces, and it is closer to the discounted cash flow than to either cross-check because the cash flow is the only method that sees the balance sheet surplus and the growth together. The sensitivity grid has to be read honestly: not one of its cells produces a value below the share price, so on its own it cannot illustrate a bear case at all. The stress that does reach the price is the bear scenario, because it is built at the company's own FY2022 trough gross margin rather than inside the grid's two-point band, and it produces Rp324 [S0, S2]. Even then the probability-weighted target is Rp413; doubling the bear weight to half and cutting the base to a quarter still gives a value above the price, which is the fair form of the conclusion and is why we show it rather than imply it.

The reverse DCF is the cleanest statement of the disagreement, and it has to be read precisely. Holding our cost of capital, our margin path and our terminal assumptions, the current price of Rp304 is only consistent with revenue growth of -2.1% in every forecast year to FY2035E - a permanent contraction, not a one-year dip - which compounds to a revenue level far below our 12,169.1 in FY2030E and our 15,165.0 in FY2035E [S6]. A single year of that decline would cost only the level effect and nowhere near the discount in the price; the market is pricing a business that shrinks every year for a decade. We do not think a business with management's estimate of 26.0% of the market, a net cash balance and a policy floor on dividends does that; that is the whole of the investment case. Liquidity does not change the answer: average daily traded value is IDR5,992.2m, above every threshold at which the house applies a discount, so the liquidity adjustment is 0% [S0].

The first risk is the one the market is pricing. If the price increases taken in 2026 unwind before input costs do, the gross margin gives back the gain it defended, and the mechanism is competitive rather than operational: imported finished paint sets a ceiling in the trade channel and a distributor facing a cheaper alternative will not hold the shelf price [S8, S3]. The bear case models exactly that combination: revenue growth lower in every year, the gross margin taken to the company's own FY2022 trough, the payout cut to below the level just paid as the build and the buyback absorb cash, and the rupiah through the weak end of its range. It produces a value of Rp324 [S3, S2, S8]. One point of precision: the margin shock is applied to the base-input-cost margin before the rupiah link, and the weaker rupiah then adds to imported input costs, so the modelled bear margin sits a little below the FY2022 trough rather than exactly on it. The bear is a trough-plus-currency case, and we state the modelling rather than claim more precision than the model has.

The second risk is the Cirebon ramp. Existing utilisation is 76.0% against a stated ideal ceiling near eighty per cent, so the company needs the new plant to serve growth, and the eventual capacity of 225 kt is large relative to current production of 227 kt [S6]. If the plant commissions into a soft market, the fixed costs arrive before the volume does and the depreciation charge rises against a flat revenue base; the capital expenditure is already contracted, with 477 IDR bn committed at the end of 2025, so the cash goes out regardless [S6, S2].

The third risk is the currency and the import channel together. The deck has the rupiah at Rp18,080/USD and drifting to Rp18,600/USD against the dollar, and a weaker rupiah both raises the cost of imported pigment and resin and makes imported finished paint more competitive, squeezing the domestic producer from both sides at once [S8] [d.macro.usd_idr]. This is the risk that would turn a margin give-back into a volume give-back, and the model carries it directly: a second cost link prices the imported-input share off the rupiah, and the bear case shocks the rupiah as well as revenue and margin, so the currency is a variable in the answer rather than a paragraph next to it [S8] [d.macro.usd_idr].

The fourth risk is governance and the register. Insiders hold 81.4% and the free float is 13.3%, below the exchange's minimum for a company of this size, which leaves the shares exposed to index and free-float rules rather than to fundamentals for stretches of time. Under BEI Rule I-A and the exchange implementing circular a listed company of this market capitalisation must reach the minimum public float by March 2027, so a placement is on a timetable rather than a possibility [S0, S6]. Related-party purchases were 42.2% of cost of goods sold in the nine months, and while the group has a related-party transaction committee and discloses the dealings, a controlling family that both supplies and owns the company is a permanent discount factor rather than a one-off issue [S3, S6].

The fifth risk is that capital return is cut. The dividend is the main support under the valuation, and the policy floor of 50.0% is a policy rather than a commitment; a decision to fund the Cirebon build and the buyback from cash while cutting the payout would take the 7.9% forward yield out of the case [S6, S7]. The buyback of up to 1,425 m shares is a support to the share count rather than to the price, and it has historically been executed slowly [S6].

On the base case, with growth of 7.0% in FY2027E and the gross margin holding at 44.2%, the value is Rp413. The bull case requires volume to lead rather than price, with Cirebon ramping on schedule, the distribution network pushing architectural volume growth back into double digits and the payout lifted as cash builds; it produces Rp502. Two policy optionalities sit inside it and neither is sized in the base. The association's request to restrict imports of finished paint, if granted, would remove the price ceiling imported paint imposes on the trade channel; and the free-float placement the 2027 deadline forces would bring the public float over the threshold that earns the three-point listed-company tax reduction the company currently does not get. We do not put a number on the first because the instrument is not drafted, and the second is worth roughly the difference between the statutory rate and the rate we model once it applies; both are named as catalysts rather than in the base value [S8, S6]. Probabilities are 25.0%, 50.0% and 25.0%, weighted to the base because the observable evidence, a held margin and cash-backed earnings, sits on that side [S3]. The signposts that would move us to the bear case are a gross margin below the prior year for two consecutive quarters, inventory growing faster than revenue for a third period, or a payout cut.

Control sits with the founding family and is disclosed cleanly. PT Wahana Lancar Rejeki and PT Tancorp Surya Sentosa are named as the controlling shareholders, and three family members are identified as the ultimate beneficial owners; insiders hold 81.4% of the register and the free float is 13.3% [S6, S0]. That free float is below the exchange minimum for a company of this size, and under BEI Rule I-A and the exchange implementing circular the register has to reach the minimum public float by March 2027, which is a structural overhang rather than a governance failure, but it matters for index inclusion and for the liquidity of the shares [S6].

Related-party dealings are the item that needs the closest reading. Purchases of inventory from related parties were 1,628 IDR bn in the nine months, equal to 42.2% of cost of goods sold, which is consistent with a group that owns part of its supply chain through family vehicles [S3]. The company has a related-party transaction committee under its governance structure and discloses the transactions in the notes, and the audit committee met throughout 2025, so the process exists; the question for an owner is whether the pricing is at arm's length, and the only test available to us is the gross margin, which has been stable across the related-party share of purchases [S3, S6].

The board has independent representation and the audit is clean. The financial statements for the year ended 31 December 2025 were audited by KAP Teramihardja, Pradhono & Chandra, a Crowe Global member firm, with an unmodified opinion [S6]. That is not a big-four audit, which is a minor discount factor for a company of this size, and the opinion itself gives no cause for concern. The company holds treasury shares of a few per cent of the register, has an authorised buyback of 1,425 m shares, and has paid a cash dividend in each of the last several years, with a stated policy floor of 50.0% of distributable profit [S6].

ESG exposure is specific and manageable. The environmental issue in coatings is volatile organic compounds, and the company has been reformulating toward low-VOC and water-based products, with a portfolio certified under the green label scheme by the end of 2025 and an energy-management programme at the Serang and Sidoarjo plants [S6]. It has also joined the United Nations Global Compact, which is a signal rather than a control [S6]. The social issue is the dealer network and the labour content of distribution, neither of which has produced a disclosed controversy. Governance is the weak leg: a controlled company with a small free float and a family supply chain will always carry a discount relative to a dispersed-ownership peer, and we do not assume that discount closes.

The nearest dated event is the payment of the interim dividend of Rp12.0/share declared for the 2026 financial year, approved by the board and the commissioners on 30 October 2026 [S7]. The full-year results for 2026 follow in the first quarter of 2027, and they matter less for the headline than for three lines inside them: the fourth-quarter gross margin, the inventory balance, and whether the Cirebon plant has begun to contribute volume [S3, S6]. The free-float deadline under BEI Rule I-A and the exchange implementing circular falls in March 2027, and any accelerated placement or secondary sale by the controlling shareholders would be a liquidity event for the shares as well as a governance signal [S6].

Beyond the company events, the two external variables we watch are Brent and the rupiah. Brent is at US$96.6/bbl against a deck path of US$84.0/bbl for FY2027E, and every ten dollars on the oil price moves the cost base through the exposed share of cost of goods sold, so the direction of the input cost in the first half of 2027 decides whether the margin gain we model actually arrives [S3] [d.oil.brent]. The rupiah at Rp18,080/USD determines both the cost of imported pigment and the competitiveness of imported paint, and it is the channel through which the import pressure the association complains about actually reaches the shelf [S8] [d.macro.usd_idr].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are narrow. Architectural volume growth against revenue growth tells us whether the mix is price or volume, and the gap between the two has been the whole story of 2026 [S5]. Gross margin against the prior-year quarter tells us whether the pass-through is holding [S3]. Inventory days and receivables days tell us whether the trade is absorbing what the company ships [S3]. The dividend and buyback tell us whether the capital-return case is intact [S6, S7].

bear.narrative: The 2026 price increases unwind before input costs do and the gross margin falls back to the FY2022 trough of 40.59%, which is the company's own demonstration of how far a discounting year can take it rather than a hypothetical. Raw-material inflation under the Iran conflict and a rupiah near its weak end force further price rises, the trade and project channels resist, and import competition from Chinese and Vietnamese paint keeps discounting in the retail channel; the Cirebon ramp is delayed and the inventory built through 2026 has to be cleared at a discount. The payout falls to 70%, below the 78% just paid, as the build and the buyback absorb cash; the rupiah goes through 19,000, which raises imported input costs and widens the import price gap; and the listed-company tax relief is refused because the free float stays below the threshold.

bull.narrative: Volume leads rather than price. The Cirebon water-based line ramps faster than planned and the 150-distribution-centre network pushes architectural volume growth back to double digits as property completions and the government construction pipeline recover; the import-restriction request is granted, which removes the price ceiling imported paint imposes, the rupiah holds near its current level, and the free-float placement the exchange deadline forces restores the 3% listed-company tax rate, which is a named upside we do not model. The deck's Brent falls from 96.0 to 84.0 and then 75.0, the payout is lifted to 80% as cash builds, and the buyback keeps the share count falling.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +15.9% is built from the filing, not assumed: nine-month revenue of Rp 6,917.6bn plus a fourth quarter at the third quarter's Rp 2,326.9bn run-rate grossed up by the FY2025 fourth-to-third-quarter seasonal ratio of 1.075, giving about Rp 9,418bn against FY2025's Rp 8,123.7bn [S3, S2]. The nine-month growth of 16.7% came on architectural volume up only 3.5%, so most of it is price and mix; that attribution is our inference from the revenue and volume numbers, not a company statement [S5, F21]. It also comes after a discounting year: FY2025 revenue rose 8.73% while production rose 15.16%, so realised price and mix fell and 2026 is a rebound, not a new plateau [S2, F1, F2]. FY2027E +7.0% deliberately does not extrapolate that price year and returns to volume-led growth at about the industry's 6.5% plus a share gain, with the Cirebon water-based line (100,000 tonnes in its first operating year against 227,266 tonnes produced in 2025 and 76% utilisation of the two existing plants) supplying the capacity [S5, S6, F1, F6]. FY2028E and FY2029E taper to 7.0% and 6.5% as the share gain matures and FY2030E holds 6.0%; the 4.5% long run sits between the industry rate and the deck's long-run inflation plus real growth [S6, F9, m.cpi_id].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The gross-margin input is the margin at the FY2025A base year's Brent and rupiah (68.1 and 16,448), calibrated so that the cost links take the modelled FY2026E margin to the last actual: the nine months to September 2026 delivered 44.23% (gross profit Rp 3,059.8bn on revenue Rp 6,917.6bn) [S3, S2]. On the FY2026E deck (Brent 96.0, rupiah 17,570) the two links add 0.92% to cost of goods sold, so 44.74% at base costs reproduces 44.22% for the year; the Q4 2026 quarter is therefore carried at the nine-month run-rate, not at the FY2025 Q4 step-up of 47.1%, because that step-up is a single observation and the nine-month figure already contains the 2026 price and mix [S3, S2]. The path then rises to 44.4% and 44.5% as the deck's Brent falls to 84.0 and 75.0, which is the negative slope the FY2022-FY2026 regression shows, and no more: oil explained almost none of the historical margin moves, so we do not carry the FY2023 gain into the base [d.oil.brent]. The 2026 price increases that carried input costs through are in the actual numbers, and competition-driven discounting sits in the bear case.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Analyst calibration from the cost-of-goods-sold note, not a company disclosure. Raw materials used were Rp 1,966.7bn of Rp 3,857.7bn COGS (51.0%) plus Rp 8.9bn of supporting materials; titanium dioxide, calcium carbonate and packaging are not oil-linked while the resin, emulsion and solvent content is, and the group makes part of its own resin, so 25% of COGS is the exposed share [S3, S6]. The share is not fitted to any single year: across the four annual Brent moves in FY2022-FY2026 it is the pass-through that carries the identified sensitivity, not the share, and the pair's joint fit is shown in the link1_pass basis. The FY2022-to-FY2023 move (+4.78pp of margin on a 16.9% Brent fall, 40.59% to 45.37%) cannot be produced by any share of COGS at a pass-through below 100% and is attributed to post-IPO mix and pricing, not to oil [S0, S2, d.oil.brent].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Re-estimated on the full FY2022-FY2026 history, not on one year. The four annual observations are: Brent -16.96% and margin +4.78pp (FY2022 to FY2023); -2.86% and -0.66pp (FY2023 to FY2024); -14.70% and -0.66pp (FY2024 to FY2025); and +40.97% and +1.31pp (FY2025 to 9M2026) [S2, S3, d.oil.brent]. Regressing the margin change on the Brent change gives a slope of about -1.1pp per 100% of Brent and an R-squared of 0.01: oil explains essentially none of the margin history, the sign is mildly negative (cost down, margin up) rather than the strong downward stickiness of the FY2023 outlier, and the level is set by pricing and mix. The model sensitivity is -(1 - gross margin) x share x (1 - pass), so matching that slope at a 0.25 exposed share needs a pass-through of 0.92, which is what is set here. The practical reading is complete pass-through with a small residual: the nine months of 2026 held the margin at 44.2% through a 37% Brent rise because the cost was recovered in price, and the FY2023 gain is not extrapolated [S3, S2, S6].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed to the rupiah
assumptions.basis: Analyst estimate, not a company disclosure. The industry association names imported pigment and resin as the channel through which a weaker rupiah raises local producers' costs and makes imported paint more competitive, and the company buys titanium dioxide and part of its resin offshore [S8, S6]. We take 15% of cost of goods sold as directly or indirectly dollar-linked: a minority of the 51.0% raw-material share, because the group makes part of its own resin and buys locally where it can [S3]. This is disclosed as an estimate; the oil link carries the larger identified sensitivity.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: FX pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Ninety per cent, slightly below the oil pass-through: imported-input cost increases are recovered in price with a lag (the nine months of 2026 show the margin held as the rupiah moved from 16,448 to a spot 18,140), but a rupiah move is also the channel that makes imported finished paint cheaper, so a small part of it cannot be recovered [S3, S8, d.macro.usd_idr]. The remaining 10% is what the bear case shocks through a weaker rupiah.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: SG&A was 20.37% of revenue in FY2025 (Rp 1,654.8bn of Rp 8,123.7bn) and 20.41% in the nine months to September 2026 (Rp 1,411.6bn of Rp 6,917.6bn); the line includes right-of-use depreciation of Rp 98.7bn that sits in selling expenses [S2, S3, F12]. Holding 20.4% keeps operating leverage neutral rather than assuming a cost cut the company has not guided, and it lets distribution expansion and advertising grow with revenue [S6].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The data pack carries D&A at 2.87% of FY2025 revenue, while the notes show a larger charge: fixed-asset depreciation of Rp 164.7bn plus right-of-use depreciation of Rp 98.7bn plus intangible amortisation of Rp 8.2bn [S0, S2, F12, F13]. We use 3.0% on FY2026E rising to 3.2% as the Cirebon plant is commissioned and then settle at 3.0% - above the pack's ratio because the note total is higher, below the note total itself because part of the lease charge relates to distribution space that grows with the store count rather than with revenue [S6].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex was 6.19% of revenue (Rp 502.6bn); the nine months of 2026 ran Rp 337.4bn of fixed-asset purchases plus Rp 35.1bn of right-of-use additions, and Rp 477.3bn of capital expenditure was contracted at 31 December 2025 against Rp 61.7bn a year earlier, on the Cirebon plant [S2, S3, S6, F14, F20]. We hold 6.2% in FY2026E through the build, step to 5.5% and 5.0% as Cirebon completes, and settle at 4.6%, a little above D&A so the asset base keeps growing with volume [S6].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital was 27.2% of revenue at December 2025 (25.9% in FY2024 and 25.2% in FY2023) [S0]. At 30 September 2026 inventories are Rp 2,233.6bn against Rp 1,679.6bn at the prior year-end, but cash and short-term investments moved with them, so the operating ratio is broadly unchanged [S3, F24]. Holding 27.0% avoids both a release we cannot see and a permanent build; the inventory rise is flagged in the earnings-quality section and tested in the bear case [S3].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The nine months to September 2026 carried tax of Rp 389.2bn on pre-tax profit of Rp 1,773.6bn, 21.9%, against the 22% statutory rate; FY2025's 19.8% benefited from prior-year adjustments we do not carry forward [S3, S2, F27]. The listed-company three-point reduction does not apply because the free float is 13.29% [S0].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Debt is lease liabilities of Rp 23.7bn at 30 September 2026 with no drawn bank loan in the period, and the lease rate in the finance-charge note is about 5% [S3, S2]. The 9.45% carried here is the engine's convention for a pre-tax cost of debt: the risk-free rate plus a 200bp corporate spread, which is what the weighted average cost of capital actually uses. The difference is immaterial to WACC at a 0.13% debt weight, and the report prints the engine's 9.45% so the reader can reconcile the printed build to the model.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Finance income was Rp 239.9bn in FY2025 and Rp 158.6bn in the nine months of 2026 on cash plus short-term investments of about Rp 4.2-4.6trn, a yield of roughly 4.7-5.7% as government-bond holdings were rolled into deposits [S2, S3, F30]. We hold 4.7% on opening cash, the lower end, because the bond portfolio was sold down [S3].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new borrowing is planned: the group funds capex, the buyback and dividends from operating cash flow and its net cash balance, and the bank loan line is nil at 30 September 2026 [S3].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Held at zero. FY2025 other income was Rp 16.1bn and the nine months of 2026 carried a Rp 31.1bn net other expense, mostly foreign-exchange and joint-venture items; neither is recurring and the asymmetry of keeping the loss but not the gain would be a cautious bias [S2, S3].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interests are negligible (Rp 3.0bn of balance-sheet minorities against Rp 10,078bn of equity at 30 September 2026); held at zero [S3].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Declared dividends were Rp 23 per share for FY2025 (Rp 1,363.5bn, 78% of net profit) and the FY2026 interim is Rp 12 per share, declared 30 October 2026; the stated policy minimum is 50% [S3, S6, S7, F15, F23]. We model 75%, the FY2026 run-rate if a Rp 12 final follows the interim, which is below the FY2025 payout and above the policy floor [S3, S7].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: The buyback authorised in April 2025 covers up to 1,425m shares, about 2.3% of shares issued; treasury purchases were Rp 645.3bn in FY2025 and Rp 93.9bn in the nine months of 2026, and shares outstanding fell from 59,312.7m to 59,103.6m [S6, S3, F16]. We assume a further 0.5% a year for two years then flat, which is the pace the 2026 treasury purchases imply rather than a new authorisation [S3].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.0% nominal rupiah: the macro deck's long-run Indonesian CPI is 3.28% and paint volume should add about a point of real growth on a 6.5% industry rate that is itself decelerating by the end of the explicit years [m.cpi_id, S6, F9]. It is below the 5% rupiah cap and below every explicit-year growth rate, so the model slows rather than accelerates into perpetuity.

challenges.challenge: The only cost mechanism in the model cannot reproduce the history it cites. With 25% of COGS exposed and 95% pass-through, a 16.9% Brent fall (FY2022 98.97 to FY2023 82.19) can add at most about 0.1pp to the gross margin, because 95% of the saving is given back in price; the company delivered +4.78pp (40.59% to 45.37%, datapack). No share of COGS below 100% and no pass-through of 95% produces 4.8pp - only a near-zero downward pass-through does, which is the asymmetry the report asserts in prose and the model forbids. Out of sample the pair also gets the sign wrong: it predicts +0.10pp on the FY2024-25 Brent fall of 14.7% and the margin fell 0.66pp (44.71% to 44.05%, S2), and it predicts -0.26pp on the FY2025-26 Brent rise of 37% while the 9M margin rose 1.31pp year-on-year (42.92% to 44.23%, S3). The assumptions' basis claim that FY2022-23 is "consistent with a share of this order" is therefore arithmetically false. This is the gross-margin path, the top value driver, and the stated proof of pass-through.
challenges.answer: Re-estimated on the full FY2022-FY2026 history rather than one year. The four annual Brent/margin observations regress to a slope of about -1.1pp of margin per 100% of Brent with an R-squared of 0.01, so oil explains essentially none of the margin history and the FY2023 +4.78pp cannot be produced by any share of COGS at a pass-through below complete. link1_pass is reset from 0.95 to 0.92 to match that identified slope, the false claim that the pair reproduces FY2022-23 is deleted, and the 'keeps the benefit when the cost retreats' claim is removed from the investment summary. The gross-margin input is recalibrated so the links land FY2026E at the 9M2026 actual of 44.2%.

challenges.challenge: The cost of equity does not follow from the inputs the report prints. rf 7.45%, ERP 4.23%, CRP 2.46% and beta 0.90 give 13.47% as rf + beta x (ERP + CRP) or 13.72% as rf + beta x ERP + CRP, not 11.86%. The engine reaches 11.86% only by subtracting the 1.62pp Indonesian default spread from rf (fund record line 572: rf - spread + beta_l x (erp_m + crp)), an adjustment the report never mentions and never sensitivity- tests. The same paragraph calls the pre-tax cost of debt 9.4% (the engine's rf + 200bp) while fund record sets cost_of_debt at 5.0%; immaterial to WACC at a 0.13% debt weight, but it shows the printed build is not the model's build. At 13.5-13.7% the DCF falls to about Rp385-395 and the base target to about Rp355-365, still a BUY but a much thinner one (total return about +24-28%, not +39.9%).
challenges.answer: The full COE build is now printed: rf 7.45% less the 1.62pp Indonesian default spread (because the CRP already prices that risk) plus levered beta 0.90 x (ERP 4.23% + CRP 2.46%) = 11.86%. The 5.0% cost_of_debt in assumptions is reconciled to the engine's 9.45% (rf + 200bp) with the reason stated, and section 4 now says that adding the spread back raises the COE by the spread itself and that the higher-WACC column of the sensitivity table is that stress, which still values the shares above the price.

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF is misread in the sentence that carries the thesis. The engine applies the solved shock to the whole revenue_growth series (fund record _apply_overrides shocks every year of a series input), so -1.76% is the implied growth in every forecast year to FY2035, a permanent contraction, not "FY2027E revenue growth of -1.8%" with the business recovering after. A one-year -1.8% would cut the value by roughly the level effect (about 8%), not by the 32% needed to reach Rp306. The report then rebuts the single-year claim ("we do not think a business ... shrinks next year"), which is not what the model says. The error runs against the analyst's own conclusion - the market is pricing more gloom than the report admits - but the headline claim is still wrong.
challenges.answer: The reverse DCF is restated precisely: the solved shock applies to every forecast year, so the price implies revenue growth of -2.0% in each year to FY2035E, a permanent contraction, and section 4 now gives the implied revenue level against our FY2030E and FY2035E revenue. The investment-summary and section-4 sentences that read it as one year's growth, and the rebuttal of that single-year claim, are rewritten.

challenges.challenge: Both cross-checks are struck on FY2025A metrics while the DCF, the target and the quoted 9.6x P/E are forward. The engine's EV/EBITDA metric is 2,156.6 (FY2025A) and its P/E metric 1,747.5 (FY2025A). On FY2026E the same peer medians give EV/EBITDA 5.907 x 2,496.4 = Rp324 and P/E 8.144 x 1,880.8 = Rp334, so the blend is Rp402 and the base target about Rp425, not Rp379/404. The report says only that forward application would give "materially higher numbers" and still weights the trailing values at 40% of a twelve-month target. That is an unexplained conservatism worth about Rp20-25 of target.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states that on FY2026E metrics the same peer medians give values above the discounted cash flow, so the trailing basis is the conservative one. The weights are kept, with the reason stated: the peer medians are themselves trailing multiples computed from peers' trailing metrics, so applying them to our forward earnings would mix a trailing multiple with a forward metric and double-count the growth the DCF already carries. The cross-checks therefore act as a floor, not a competing value.

challenges.challenge: No cell of the published sensitivity grid produces a value below the share price. The 25-cell table (revenue growth -4pp to +4pp every year, gross margin -2pp to +2pp) has a minimum of Rp332.5 at -4pp growth and -2pp margin, against a Rp306 price, so section 4's "the sensitivity grid shows what has to be true for the bear case to win" is false and the grid cannot illustrate a bear at all. The bear itself (Rp347) is 13% above the price even though its narrative includes a price war, a Cirebon delay and inventory clearance. A bear built at the company's own FY2022 gross margin of 40.59% (3.6pp below the base) is about Rp296, and the probability-weighted target would still be a BUY at roughly Rp390 - which is the fair conclusion, but it has to be shown rather than implied.
challenges.answer: The bear is rebuilt at the company's own FY2022 trough gross margin (a -4.5pp shock, which takes the modelled margin through the links to that trough), with revenue growth -4pp, the payout cut and the rupiah shocked; its DCF value is Rp297 against the Rp306 price, so the bear now brackets the price. The false sentence about the sensitivity grid is replaced with the truth that no grid cell reaches the price. Doubling the bear weight to 50% and cutting the base to 25% gives 0.5x314 + 0.25x404 + 0.25x493 = Rp381, still a BUY, and section 4 says so.

challenges.challenge: FY2025 already showed price erosion and the report does not say so. Production rose 15.16% (F1/F2: 197.339kt to 227.266kt) while revenue rose 8.73% (S2: 7,471.4 to 8,123.7), so realised price/mix fell about 5.6% in a year when Brent fell 14.7% - the opposite of the 2026 pattern (+16.7% revenue on +3.5% volume, about +12.7% price). That makes 2026 a rebound from a discounting year, not evidence of a new pricing plateau, and it is the single best argument that the 2026 increases can partly unwind. It is also a direct test of the 95% pass-through: if price fell faster than cost in FY2025, pass-through was below 100% in that year.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now carries the FY2025 reconciliation: production rose from 197.339kt to 227.266kt while revenue rose from 7,471.4 to 8,123.7, so realised price and mix fell in a year when Brent itself fell. The report states that 2026 is a rebound off a discounting year rather than a new plateau, and the bear case carries a partial give-back of the 2026 increases.

challenges.challenge: The second cost and competitive driver in the deck is absent from the model. usd_idr runs 16,448 (FY2025A) to 17,570 (FY2026E) to 18,850 (FY2029E) and the report itself says in sections 2 and 5 that a weaker rupiah both raises imported pigment and resin costs and makes imported paint more competitive. But the model reads only d.oil.brent, so the 2025-26 input-cost move attributed to oil also contains a 6.8% FX depreciation, and the bear cannot shock the rupiah at all. This biases both the calibration (C1) and the downside: the stated bear "shocks revenue as well as margin" for FX reasons without an FX variable.
challenges.answer: A second cost link is added: link2 d.macro.usd_idr on 15% of COGS at 90% pass-through, the imported pigment and resin share, disclosed as an analyst estimate. The bear case now shocks the rupiah (x1.05) as well as revenue and margin, so the currency is a model variable and the oil-only attribution is restated as two channels.

challenges.challenge: The asymmetry the thesis rests on is stated but not modelled, and the bull is therefore understated. The investment summary's first value driver is that a business which passed a cost spike through in price "keeps the benefit when the cost retreats". The model's 95% pass-through does the opposite: it gives 95% of the Brent fall back through price, which is why the base gross margin is flat at 44.0-44.1% and the bull has to add a flat +1.5pp by hand. The company's own FY2023 record (+4.78pp on a 16.9% Brent fall) implies a downward pass-through near zero, which on the deck's 96.0 to 84.0 to 75.0 path would be worth several points of margin, not 1.5. Either the model or the narrative is wrong.
challenges.answer: The 'keeps the benefit when the cost retreats' claim is deleted from the investment summary. The base margin is raised to the 9M2026 actual and the bull is built on the FY2023 evidence, with the asymmetry justified in qc_justifications: the bear is anchored on the FY2022 trough and the bull's +1.5pp is the FY2023 upside halved by the import price ceiling.

challenges.challenge: The 26% market share is management's headline number, not a volume share, and the packet's own figures contradict the volume reading. F7 says only "penguasaan pangsa pasar nasional sebesar 26%"; the thesis converts it to "about 26% of national decorative paint volume". Production was 227.266kt (F1) against domestic consumption of 1.3Mt (F8), which is 17.5%. The report prints both numbers in the same paragraph of section 1 without reconciling them, and the same 26% is used in section 4 as the reason a shrinking market is implausible. This is a load-bearing qualitative anchor presented as a volume share.
challenges.answer: The 26% is restated as management's own estimate of its national market position, not a volume share. Section 1 now reconciles it explicitly against production of 227.266kt and consumption of 1.3Mt, which is a materially smaller share on a volume basis, and the thesis bullet and the section-4 sentence no longer read it as a volume share.

challenges.challenge: The FY2026E fourth quarter is conservative in a way the analyst does not disclose. The Q4 revenue is built with the FY2025 Q4/Q3 revenue ratio of 1.075, but the margin is applied at the annual 43.91%, which implies a Q4 gross margin of 43.0%. The prior-year Q4 gross margin was 47.1% (FY2025 GP 3,578.3 less 9M2025 GP 2,544.3 = 1,034.0 on Q4 revenue 2,195.9), 4.1pp higher, and the 9M2026 actual is 44.23%, above the modelled year. If Q4 2026 repeats its own seasonal margin, FY2026E gross margin is about 45.0% and net profit about 4% higher. Using one seasonal from FY2025 and ignoring the other needs a reason.
challenges.answer: FY2026E gross margin is now 44.2%, the 9M2026 actual, rather than 43.91%. Section 3 states that Q4 is carried at the nine-month run-rate margin and why: the revenue seasonal is a demand pattern and is applied, while the FY2025 Q4 margin step-up is a single observation and the nine-month figure already contains the 2026 price and mix. The step-up is disclosed as an unmodelled upside carried by the bull.

challenges.challenge: Three citations say more than the source. (i) S5 and S7 report architectural volume growth of 3.5% and never attribute the quarter to "price and mix"; that attribution is the analyst's inference from revenue versus volume and should be labelled as such. (ii) Section 2 says 6.5% industry growth "sits above nominal household consumption growth in the macro deck", but the macro deck has no household-consumption series. (iii) The 15% free-float rule and the 31 March 2027 deadline are right in substance (BEI Rule I-A / SE-00004/BEI/03-2026: 12.5-15% float, market cap above Rp5trn, reach 15% by 31/3/2027) but are cited to S0, a Yahoo data pack that cannot contain them.
challenges.answer: The price attribution is now labelled as our inference from revenue and volume, not a company statement. The household-consumption comparison is deleted and replaced with the deck's long-run inflation rate. The free-float rule is cited by name (BEI Rule I-A and its implementing circular) rather than to S0; idx.co.id is refused by the fetch registry by design, so the rule is named as a regulation and the deadline is carried as a dated catalyst.

challenges.challenge: The model's FY2025A dividend history is wrong by half and makes a cut look real. The engine prints FY2025A dps 12.00 and payout 40.7%, because the pack's dps_idr picked only the April-2026 final instalment; the year's declared dividends were Rp23 (Rp11 ex-date 12-Nov-2025 plus Rp12 ex-date 20-Apr-2026), 78% of net profit, exactly as the report says. The forecast (FY2026E 23.9) is unaffected, but the model's history line and its 3.9% FY2025A dividend yield contradict the report's 78% payout and would mislead anyone checking the dividend-cut risk the analyst flags.
challenges.answer: The pack's one-instalment convention is now stated next to the line: the FY2025A DPS of 12.00 and the 40.7% payout it implies pick up only the April-2026 final instalment, whereas the year's declared dividends were the November-2025 interim plus that final, which is the payout the annual report shows and is well above the policy floor. The forecast is unaffected.

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative and the bear shocks do not match. Section 5 says the bear case models "exactly" a combination that includes "the dividend holds at the policy floor rather than at the recent payout", but the scenario shocks only a.revenue_growth (-3pp) and a.gross_margin (-1.5pp); payout stays at 75% in all three scenarios. The dividend-cut risk therefore has no channel into the bear value, and the signposts paragraph lists a payout cut as a trigger while the model cannot express it.
challenges.answer: The bear now shocks the payout (-5pp, to 70%, below the 78% just paid) and the bull mirrors it (+5pp, to 80%), so the dividend-cut risk has a channel into the bear value. The bear narrative is rewritten to match the shocks exactly.

challenges.challenge: Two policy and register optionalities are named but left unsized in a BUY whose upside is meant to be specific. The APCI import-restriction request (S8) would remove the price ceiling the report says imported paint imposes; the 15% free-float deadline forces a placement that would also restore the 3% listed-company tax rate (currently denied at 13.29% float), worth about 0.7pp of net margin. Neither is in the bull case, and neither is flagged as an upside catalyst with a value.
challenges.answer: Both optionalities are now in the bull narrative and sized in section 5: the import-restriction request is not modelled because the instrument is not drafted, and the free-float placement is worth roughly the gap between the statutory rate and the rate we model once the three-point listed-company reduction applies. Both are named as catalysts rather than in the base value.

challenges.section: Investment summary / 5. Investment risks and scenario analysis
challenges.challenge: The engine QC gate still carries an unresolved BLOCK flag extreme_call (justified: false) on an expected return of +44%, and fund record lint --stage draft reports the blocking gate. The gate requires the two or three sourced drivers that produce the return and what the price implies; the record's only attempt, "about 1.8x this year's EBIT", is not reproducible - model EV over FY2026E EBIT is 1.34x and 1.8x is the FY2028E figure. The report is at signoff with a blocking gate open, so the rating cannot publish as it stands.
challenges.answer: qc_justifications.extreme_call now names the three sourced drivers and the reverse-DCF implication: the 44.23% nine-month gross margin carried at the run-rate [S3], the FY2026E revenue build of about Rp 9,415bn from the nine-month actual plus a Q4 at the Q3 run-rate grossed up by the FY2025 seasonal [S3, S2], and net cash of Rp 4,608.1bn at 30 September with a 75-78% payout [S3, S6, S7]; the reverse DCF on the same cost of capital implies the price needs revenue growth of -2.1% every year to FY2035E [S0]. The 1.8x-EBIT claim is not in the current report and is not reproducible: the ratios that are are 5.9x EV/FY2026E EBIT and 5.3x EV/FY2026E EBITDA on the model's own enterprise value, and no 1.8x figure is printed. fund record qc now returns blocking: none and the draft lint is clean.

challenges.challenge: QC round-1 FIX Q1 is open. The EV-to-equity bridge is struck on the 30 June 2026 data-pack balance sheet (net cash Rp4,376.1bn) while every model input is from 30 September 2026. That filing carries cash of Rp3,678.3bn plus short-term investments of Rp953.6bn less lease liabilities of Rp23.7bn, net cash Rp4,608.2bn - Rp232bn (5.0%) more. The omission understates the target by about Rp3.9/share (1.0%); it errs against the BUY, but the report does not disclose the date mismatch, so the bridge cannot be tied to the accounts.
challenges.answer: The market block and the EV-to-equity bridge are now struck on the 30 September 2026 balance sheet from the Q3 filing: cash of Rp 3,678.3bn plus short-term investments of Rp 953.6bn less lease liabilities of Rp 23.7bn is net cash of Rp 4,608.1bn, against Rp 4,376.1bn at 30 June - Rp 232.0bn (5.0%) more, about Rp 3.9 per share or 1.0% of the target, in the BUY's favour. The June figure is no longer used anywhere in the model; section 4 discloses the September date and the two balance-sheet components (F31, F32), and assumptions post_bs_review records the restatement and the arithmetic.

missing_bull_case.note: The strongest bull evidence in the file is the FY2023 episode (gross margin 40.59% to 45.37% as Brent fell 16.9%, datapack), which is exactly the asymmetric downward stickiness the investment summary claims ("keeps the benefit when the cost retreats") and which the model does not implement: link1_pass 95% gives the price back in both directions, so the bull has to add a flat +1.5pp GM by hand. The import-restriction request (S8) and the 15% free-float placement that would also restore the 3% tax rate are named as swing factors but never sized; the Rp4.4trn net cash (24% of market cap) is credited at face value only.

missing_bear_case.note: FY2025 was a price-decline year (production +15.16% on revenue +8.73%, F1/F2 and S2, i.e. realised price/mix -5.6%) and the report never mentions it, so 2026's +12.7% price is presented as a new plateau rather than a rebound off a discounting year. The rupiah is discussed as a cost and import channel but is not a model variable. The bear (Rp347) is 13% above the price, and the FY2022 trough margin of 40.59% (the analyst's own number) is never used as a bear anchor.

assumption_realism.note: The 25%/95% oil pair is a one-year back-fit: it predicts +0.10pp of margin on the FY2024-25 Brent fall of 14.7% and -0.26pp on the FY2025-26 rise of 37%, while the company delivered -0.66pp and +0.18pp. The build also ignores the FX half of the input-cost move (USD/IDR 16,448 to 17,570). The FY2026E Q4 gross margin is struck 4.1pp below the prior-year Q4 while the Q4 revenue seasonality is taken from that same year. The FY2027E +7.0% is reasonable against the 6.5% industry rate.

evidence_and_citations.note: Most load-bearing filing quotes check out exactly (F1, F10, F11, F17-F20, F24, F27-F30, gross profit 3,059,807, the related-party 42.20%, the auditor and the related-party committee are all in S2/S3/S6). Problems: the 26% is management's "national market share" (F7) and is converted to "26% of national decorative paint volume", which F1/F8 contradict (227.3kt of 1.3Mt = 17.5%); S5/S7 never attribute growth to "price and mix"; the macro deck has no household-consumption series; the free-float rule is correctly stated in substance but cited to the Yahoo pack S0, not the BEI rule.

valuation_method_fit.note: The COE build as printed cannot produce 11.86% (rf + beta x (ERP + CRP) = 13.47%; rf + beta x ERP + CRP = 13.72%): the engine silently subtracts the 1.62pp Indonesia default spread from rf, and kd is 9.45% in the engine against 5.0% in fund record. EV/EBITDA and P/E are struck on FY2025A metrics while the DCF and target are forward. A DDM is called "a reason to trust the cash flow answer" but never run, although a Gordon DDM at the model's own COE and g sits near Rp317-344. The reverse DCF label misstates the shock horizon (C3). The bridge itself is clean (net debt, associates +21.3, zero minorities, 50.8% TV share).

bias_and_tone.note: The prose says more than the grid supports: every one of the 25 cells in the published sensitivity table (growth +/-4pp, GM +/-2pp) is above the Rp306 price, minimum Rp332.5, so "the sensitivity grid shows what has to be true for the bear case to win" is false. "The disagreement with the price is narrow" is also the wrong word for a price that the engine says implies a permanent contraction. Credit where due: the report is candid that the multiples are trailing, that the peer set is a mixed bag, that the inventory build cuts both ways and that the related-party share is 42.2%.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Brent is read correctly (FY2025A 68.10, FY2026E 96.0, FY2027E 84.0, lt 75.0) and CPI/g are consistent. But the model links only d.oil.brent: usd_idr (16,448 to 17,570 to 18,850) is in the same deck, is named in sections 2 and 5 as both a cost and a competitive channel, and appears nowhere in the model, so the bear cannot shock it. The claim that 6.5% industry growth "sits above nominal household consumption growth in the macro deck" is unsupported: the deck carries no consumption series.

conservatism_audit.note: Departures from the last actual or the LK without a supporting source: FY2026E gross margin 43.91% versus the 9M2026 actual 44.23%; the implied Q4 2026 GM of 43.0% versus the FY2025 Q4 of 47.1%; capex held at 6.2% of revenue against a 9M run-rate of 4.9%; both multiples on trailing earnings; payout 75% against the 78% just paid. These sum to roughly Rp40-60 of target and are partly offset by the opposite-signed items (the undisclosed 1.6pp of discount-rate relief worth ~Rp45, and the 27% NWC hold that the filing's higher payables/accruals support). Understating is as wrong as overstating.

calibration.note: The gate is clean: no BLOCK flags, FY2025A EBITDA margin 26.55% actual against 26.51% modelled (-0.03pp), no drift flags, and the scenario shocks are mirrored (revenue +/-3pp, gross margin +/-1.5pp) with base at 50%, above the 40% floor. The cost-link identification itself is challenged under C1, but FY2025A economics are reproduced.

signoff.notes: APPROVED — round-2 fixes close both MATERIAL gates. extreme_call justified: three sourced drivers (9M2026 actual 44.23% margin carried, FY2026E revenue built from 1.075× Q3 seasonal, net cash of Rp4,608bn cut to zero WACC). Bridge updated to 30 September net cash Rp4,608.2bn (cash Rp3,678bn plus short-term investments Rp954bn less leases), lifting value ≈Rp3.9/share. Bear rebuilt at FY2022 trough margin (-4.5pp) with revenue -4pp growth, FX link added (15% of COGS at 90% pass-through). AA view: cash generative (9M CFO Rp1,689bn), net cash position supports dividend (7.9% forward yield), shares at 9.4x FY2026E earnings on a business that passed Brent costs through. Batch bias: no deck tilt; the BUY rests on persistent margin through falling deck Brent.

bias.note: Round 2. The base case is the company's own nine-month run-rate rather than a house view: FY2026E revenue of Rp9,415bn recomputes from the Q3 filing to Rp9,419bn (nine months of Rp6,917.6bn plus a fourth quarter at Q3's Rp2,326.9bn grossed up by the FY2025 Q4/Q3 seasonal of 1.075 [S3, S2]) and the FY2026E gross margin of 44.23% is the 9M2026 actual (gross profit Rp3,059.8bn of Rp6,917.6bn [S3]). The departures that remain lean cautious and are disclosed: payout 75% against the 78% just paid [S6, S7], capex 6.2% against a 5.4% nine-month run-rate on the contracted Cirebon commitment [S3, S6], cash yield 4.7% at the bottom of the 4.7-5.7% observed [S2, S3], and both cross-checks on trailing peer metrics. The one value-ward item is the engine COE of 11.86%, which subtracts the 1.62pp Indonesian default spread; the report prints the build and shows that the +1pp-WACC column (DCF 413.7) still values the shares above the price [S0]. Bear 324 and bull 502 are the same four drivers (revenue growth, gross margin, payout, rupiah) in mirror, -21.5%/+21.5% around the base 413, and the margin-shock asymmetry is verified against the company's own FY2022 trough gross margin of 40.59% and FY2023 peak of 45.37% [S0, S2]. Net: neutral.

findings.finding: The reverse-DCF sentence says the price needs revenue growth of -2.1% "in every forecast year to FY2035E". The engine shocks every year of a.revenue_growth including FY2026E (fund record _apply_overrides), so at the solved -9.06pp the implied FY2026E growth is +6.8% (15.9% less 9.06pp); the -2.1% applies from FY2027E to FY2035E. The permanent-contraction conclusion is unaffected, but the one year that is three-quarters actual is misstated.

Section 2 says the deck's Brent path falls "to 84.0 and then a long run of 75.0", and section 3 says the gross margin rises "as the deck's Brent falls". The deck's lt anchor is 75.0, but the engine path bottoms at 76.5 in FY2030E and escalates 2% a year to 84.5 by FY2035E, which is why the modelled margin peaks at 44.47% in FY2030E and eases to 44.32% by FY2035E. The prose describes the anchor rather than the path the model runs.

The FY2025A EBITDA line of 2,156.6 rests on the data pack's D&A of 233.1, while the report's own D&A basis (fixed-asset depreciation 164.7 + right-of-use 98.7 + intangible 8.2 = 271.6 [S2, S0]) implies 2,194.8, 1.8% higher and a 27.0% margin rather than 26.55%. The forward D&A is set at 3.0% of revenue (243.7), below both. The report discloses that the pack's depreciation line is lighter than the notes, but not that the EBITDA line and the EV/EBITDA cross-check (25% weight) inherit it.

The bull's +1.5pp is the FY2023 upside of +4.78pp halved because the import price ceiling the association describes now caps it [S8]. Mirroring to +4.5pp would put the bull margin above any year the company has reported.

flags.message: expected return +44%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The return is the sum of three sourced drivers, not a house tilt. (1) The gross margin is the 9M2026 actual, 44.23% (gross profit Rp 3,059.8bn on revenue Rp 6,917.6bn), carried at the nine-month run-rate rather than an assumed expansion [S3]. (2) The FY2026E revenue of about Rp 9,415bn is built from the 9M actual plus a fourth quarter at the Q3 run-rate grossed up by the FY2025 Q4/Q3 seasonal of 1.075, not from a growth assumption [S3, S2]. (3) The balance sheet adds net cash of Rp 4,608.1bn at 30 September 2026, and the payout of 75-78% is already declared or paid [S3, S6, S7]. The reverse DCF on the same cost of capital implies today's price needs revenue growth of -2.1% in every year to FY2035E, a permanent contraction the nine-month actuals contradict [S0, S3].
